summary: Sets out the IESG's policy on character sets and languages in Internet protocols, to guide standardization work in the IETF. Among its requirements is support for UTF-8. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: It is a rule that says Internet protocols should work with writing from all the world's languages, not just English.

questions: what is the ietf policy on character sets
do ietf protocols have to support utf-8
what is the i-default language tag
subtitle: The IETF rule that protocols must handle UTF-8, label the charset, and carry language tags.

tldr.problem: The Internet is international, so protocols must exchange text in many languages and characters, but IETF protocols handled this inconsistently.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG policy requires protocols to identify the charset of all character data, to be able to use UTF-8, to carry language information for text, and to support language negotiation where users are shown text.
tldr.outcome: Lack of UTF-8 support is a violation of the policy and needs a variance procedure with clear justification to enter or advance on the standards track.

today: RFC 2277 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the policy text as published in January 1998.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC opens with a blunt premise: the Internet is international, so there is an absolute requirement to interchange data in many languages, which use a bewildering number of characters. The document records the policy the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) applies to standardization work in the IETF.

It is based on the recommendations of the IAB Character Set Workshop of February 29 to March 1, 1996, documented in RFC 2130. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119, and apply to protocols submitted to the IETF standards process.
sections.eli5: People all over the world use the Internet, so its rules need to work for every kind of writing.

sections.title: Where to Do Internationalization
sections.content:
Internationalization is for humans, so protocols are not subject to it; text strings are. Where protocol elements look like text tokens, a protocol MUST specify which parts are protocol and which are text.

Names are called a problem: people feel strongly about them, many are for local use, and they tend to leak out of the local context. RFC 1958 recommends US-ASCII for all globally visible names. The policy does not mandate how names are internationalized, but requires every protocol to describe whether its names are internationalized or US-ASCII.

In an application's protocol stack, usually one or a few layers address these problems. Working groups must make sure that when the job is left to another layer, the people responsible for that layer know they have it.
sections.eli5: The commands a computer sends are like fixed button labels. Only the words meant for people need to be translated, and someone must be in charge of that.

sections.title: Charsets and UTF-8
sections.content:
The RFC uses charset to mean a set of rules for mapping a sequence of octets to a sequence of characters, such as a coded character set combined with a character encoding scheme. It is the identifier used in MIME charset= parameters and registered in the IANA charset registry. A name is an identifier such as a person's name, hostname, domain name, filename or e-mail address.

All protocols MUST identify, for all character data, which charset is in use. Protocols MUST be able to use the UTF-8 charset (ISO 10646 with the UTF-8 encoding scheme) for all text. They MAY also specify other charsets or encodings such as UTF-16, but being unable to use UTF-8 violates the policy and would need a variance procedure with clear and solid justification before entering or advancing on the standards track.

Existing protocols, or protocols moving data from existing datastores, may need other charsets or even a non-UTF-8 default. That is acceptable as long as UTF-8 support is possible. Any other charset MUST be registered in the IANA charset registry, if necessary when the protocol is published.
sections.eli5: Every message must say which alphabet code it uses, and every tool must be able to speak the one code that covers all the world's letters, called UTF-8.

sections.title: Deciding a Charset
sections.content:
When a protocol allows several charsets, someone must choose. Where producer and consumer talk directly, as with HTTP, it may make sense to negotiate a charset before sending data. Where they do not, as with e-mail or stored data, the best one can do is label the charset clearly and pick one that is as widely known as possible.

A charset is an absolute: text in it cannot be rendered comprehensibly without supporting that charset. This applies even to English, since charsets like EBCDIC do not have ASCII as a proper subset.

Negotiating a charset may be seen as an interim mechanism until UTF-8 interchange is prevalent, but the RFC warns that the interim may last at least 50 years, so it should be thought of as permanent in practice.
sections.eli5: If two people can talk, they can agree on a language first. If you leave a note for someone, you must label the language and pick one many people can read.

sections.title: Language Tagging and Negotiation
sections.content:
All human-readable text has a language, and knowing it helps with formatting, text-to-speech, searching, hyphenation and spellchecking. Machines usually cannot deduce the language, so the protocol must say how to transfer it.

Protocols that transfer text MUST provide for carrying the language of that text, and SHOULD do so for names where appropriate. This does not mean the information must always be present; it means a well-defined way to carry it must exist. Protocols SHOULD use the RFC 1766 language tag, or justify doing otherwise. A language is distinct from a POSIX locale, which identifies cultural conventions.

Protocols where users have text presented in response to their actions MUST support multiple languages. This may be a negotiation where the client proposes languages and the server picks one, or a server sending several variants for the client to choose from. The RFC calls language negotiation a permanent requirement.

When the sender does not know the recipient's preferences, such as login failures, e-mailed warnings or before negotiation, text SHOULD be in the Default Language, tagged i-default. Such messages MUST be understandable by an English-speaking person. Negotiating English is not the same thing: Default Language is an emergency measure.
sections.eli5: Writing should say which language it is in, so a computer can read it aloud or sort it correctly. If a program does not know your language, it uses a plain message that an English reader can follow.

sections.title: Locale and Documenting Decisions
sections.content:
A POSIX locale bundles collating order, date format, currency format and similar conventions. The policy does not require sending locale information on all text, but encourages it when appropriate, for instance where the user is expected to process the text. The recipient may agree with the sender's locale or ignore it. A locale tag such as no_NO.iso-8859-1 contains both language and charset, so care is needed to define which specification applies. The default locale is the POSIX locale.

Documents that deal with internationalization at all SHOULD collect a synopsis of their approach into a section called "Internationalization considerations", placed next to the Security Considerations section.
sections.eli5: A locale is a bundle of local habits, like how dates and money are written. You may share it, but the reader does not have to follow it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC identifies little security impact. It notes only that security warnings in a foreign language may cause inappropriate behaviour from the user, and that multilingual systems usually have problems with consistency between language variants. No other relevant security considerations were identified.
sections.eli5: If a warning is written in a language you cannot read, you might do the wrong thing, so languages need to match up.
